title: Reading the Ground: Bearing, Settlement and the Geotechnical Report
summary: A shallow foundation spreads a building's load onto soil near the surface. Two limits govern it: the soil must not fail in shear, and the building must not settle too much or too unevenly. This lesson teaches how to read a geotechnical report, why settlement usually governs, and when ground improvement makes sense.
body:
A foundation has two jobs: stop the ground from failing, and stop the building from moving more than it can tolerate. On most sites the second job, settlement, decides the design long before the first one does.

Recall

Q. Under United States excavation safety rules, what is a competent person?

A. Someone who can identify existing and predictable hazards on site and has the authority to take prompt corrective action.

Q. What is the last responsible moment in design?

A. The latest point at which a decision can be made without closing off a better option or forcing rework.

Q. What are the four jobs of a fire strategy?

A. Detect, suppress, contain, and get people out.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, the foundation is the one part of a building you can almost never fix cheaply later. A cracked partition can be patched; a footing that settled 50 millimetres more than its neighbour cannot be lifted without underpinning, which costs many times the original foundation. The geotechnical report is the document that tells your structural engineer what the ground can do. If you can read it, you can ask the questions that decide whether the foundation is simple, expensive or dangerous.

Two limits: bearing and settlement

In plain English: push hard enough on soil and it gives way, sliding out from under the footing. Push less hard and it does not give way, but it still squeezes down, slowly, like a sponge. The first is a strength limit. The second is a movement limit.

The professional terms are bearing capacity and settlement. Ultimate bearing capacity is the pressure at which the soil beneath a footing fails in shear. The geotechnical engineer divides it by a factor of safety, commonly in the range of about 2.5 to 3 by practice, to give an allowable bearing pressure for strength. Settlement is the downward movement of the footing under load. Some happens quickly as the building is loaded; in clays, more happens over months or years as water is squeezed out of the soil, which is called consolidation. The structural engineer cares most about differential settlement: the difference in movement between two footings, because that is what bends the frame and cracks the finishes.

The design allowable bearing pressure in the report is the lower of the strength value and the value that keeps settlement within a stated limit. On soft or variable ground the settlement value is usually lower, and it governs.

Worked example. A hypothetical report states that a stiff clay has an ultimate bearing capacity of 600 kilopascals beneath a 2-metre-wide footing. With a factor of safety of 3, the strength allowable is 200 kilopascals. But the report also says that to keep total settlement within 25 millimetres for footings up to 3 metres wide, the pressure must not exceed 150 kilopascals. The design value is 150. A designer who used 200 would make the footings about a quarter smaller and the building would likely settle more than the frame can tolerate.

Say that out loud now.

Reading the report

A geotechnical report has two halves: what was found, and what is recommended. Read both, and read them in that order.

What was found sits in the boring logs and test results. A boring log records, at each depth, the soil type, its colour and moisture, any groundwater met, and test results such as the standard penetration test (SPT) blow count, the number of hammer blows needed to drive a sampler a set distance, which is a rough index of density or stiffness. Laboratory tests on samples add moisture content, strength and consolidation properties. Look at three things: how many borings, how deep they go, and whether they agree. A building's load stresses the soil to a depth of roughly one and a half to two times the footing width, and much deeper under a wide mat or a group of closely spaced footings, so borings that stop short of that depth have not described the soil the building will load.

What is recommended sits in the design section: the foundation type, the bearing pressure, the founding depth, the expected settlement, groundwater and dewatering advice, fill and compaction specifications, and any conditions such as removal of unsuitable soil. Every recommendation should trace back to the logs. If the report recommends a value that no test in the logs supports, ask why.

When the ground is not good enough

If the ground near the surface cannot carry the load within the settlement limit, there are three broad paths. Spread the load more widely, by bigger footings or a mat foundation, a single thick slab under the whole building. Improve the ground, by removing and replacing poor soil with compacted fill, by compaction from the surface, by stone columns or rigid inclusions installed into the soil, or by preloading, placing a temporary surcharge of soil to squeeze out settlement before building. Or bypass the poor ground with deep foundations such as piles, which is next week's subject.

Second worked example. A hypothetical site has 3 metres of soft fill over stiff clay. Option A: excavate the fill under the building footprint and replace it with engineered compacted fill, about 1,500 cubic metres at a hypothetical 60 dollars per cubic metre all in, about 90,000 dollars, plus a few weeks. Option B: found the footings through the fill onto the clay with deepened footings or short piers, perhaps 140,000 dollars. Option C: piles, perhaps 400,000 dollars. The geotechnical engineer's settlement estimate for each option, not the price alone, decides which is acceptable.

Compaction testing

Fill is only as good as its compaction. The specification states a target, usually a percentage of the soil's maximum dry density measured in a laboratory test, the Proctor test, under ASTM D698 or the modified version ASTM D1557. In the field, technicians measure the density of each layer, often with a nuclear density gauge under ASTM D6938 or a sand cone under ASTM D1556, and compare it with the target. A failed test means rework of that layer before the next goes on. Verify against the current adopted edition of each standard.

How the best do it

The strongest owners scope the site investigation with the geotechnical engineer after the building's layout and loads are roughly known, rather than ordering a fixed number of borings before design. They phase it: a preliminary investigation for feasibility, then a design investigation targeted at the actual footprint and load. And on important or difficult sites they pay for an independent geotechnical review. A small developer can copy all three: ask the geotechnical engineer to set boring locations and depths against a preliminary layout, budget for a second phase, and get a short peer review of the foundation recommendations.

Six-Lens Check

Tax: ground improvement and foundation costs are generally part of the building's capital cost; ask your tax adviser how they are classified. Liability: the geotechnical engineer's report is relied on by others, so check the reliance language and their professional liability insurance. Banking: lenders will want the report and may require a reliance letter in their name. Governance: record who approved the foundation type and the risk accepted. Estate: the report and compaction records are part of the asset's permanent file. Exit: a buyer's engineer will ask for the report, the settlement monitoring and any remediation.

Professional sign-off required: licensed geotechnical engineer, for bearing pressure, settlement and fill specifications; structural engineer of record, for footing design and tolerable movement.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is an investigation too shallow or too sparse for the building that was eventually designed, often because it was ordered before the layout existed. The control is to re-scope the investigation once loads are known, and to have the geotechnical engineer confirm in writing that the borings cover the stressed depth beneath every footing.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner reads only the bearing pressure and skips the settlement estimate and the conditions. The number is the least of the report. The conditions, such as removing unsuitable soil or controlling groundwater, are where the cost lives.

Callback

In Week 31, Pax and Cole taught desk due diligence, including geotechnical screening before purchase. The design investigation is the second, deeper look. A site bought on a desk study that said "suitable for shallow foundations" has not yet been proved suitable for your building's loads.

Recap

A shallow foundation must not fail the ground and must not settle too much or too unevenly; settlement usually governs. Read the report's findings before its recommendations, and check borings reach the stressed depth. Where ground is poor, spread the load, improve the ground or bypass it. Fill is proven only by compaction tests against a stated target.

Next: Ford on Failure Forensics: the Transcona Grain Elevator, which tipped over on its foundation in 1913.
checklist: I read the boring logs before the recommendations.
I check that borings reach the depth stressed by each footing.
I know the design bearing pressure and whether strength or settlement governs it.
I know the predicted total and differential settlement and what the frame can tolerate.
I re-scope the investigation once the layout and loads are known.
I see compaction test results for every fill layer before the next is placed.
I have a reliance letter for the report in my name and my lender's.
head: Field checklist
speak: A shallow foundation has two limits. Bearing capacity is the pressure at which the soil fails in shear; the geotechnical engineer divides it by a factor of safety to get an allowable value. Settlement is how far the footing moves, and in clays it continues as water is squeezed out. What cracks a building is differential settlement between footings. The design pressure is the lower of the strength value and the settlement value, and settlement usually governs. In my example the strength allowable was 200 kilopascals but settlement limited it to 150. I read the boring logs before the recommendations, and I check that the borings reach the depth the footings stress, roughly one and a half to two footing widths and more under a mat. Poor ground can be spread, improved or bypassed with piles. Fill is proven only by compaction tests against a stated percentage of laboratory maximum density.
terms: Allowable bearing pressure — the soil pressure a foundation may apply, limited by both a factor of safety against shear failure and a settlement limit.
Differential settlement — the difference in settlement between two parts of a foundation, which bends the structure and cracks finishes.
Consolidation — the slow settlement of a clay as water is squeezed out of it under load.

hostile.q: The report gives 150 kilopascals, but your contractor says the clay looks stiff and 200 would be fine. Why not save the concrete?
hostile.a: Because 150 is the settlement limit, not the strength limit. The clay may well carry 200 without failing, but the geotechnical engineer has calculated that above 150 our footings would settle more than the frame can tolerate. A visual judgment in an excavation does not replace that calculation. If the contractor believes the ground is better, the route is a request to the geotechnical engineer with evidence, not a change on site.

title: Transcona 1913: The Elevator That Lay Down on Its Foundation
summary: In October 1913 the newly built Transcona Grain Elevator near Winnipeg tilted dramatically as it was first filled with grain, because the clay beneath its foundation failed in bearing. The structure itself survived and was later righted on deeper foundations. Ford takes it through seven steps and draws one rule.
body:
At Transcona the building was strong and the ground was not. The foundation pressed on clay that nobody had properly examined at the depth the load reached, and when the load arrived, the ground gave way.

Recall

Q. What usually governs the allowable bearing pressure on soft or variable ground?

A. Settlement, not strength: the pressure is limited so that total and differential settlement stay within what the structure can tolerate.

Q. What does Rule 108 say?

A. Never let a change of use, load or layout pass a stage gate, or reach site, until the structural engineer of record has re-checked the whole structure for it and confirmed in writing that it works.

Q. What is a firestop?

A. A tested system that seals an opening or penetration through a fire-rated wall or floor so it keeps its rating.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Transcona is the classic bearing failure: clear, well studied, and on Canadian soil. It is useful precisely because the structure did not fail. The engineering above ground was sound. The failure was entirely in what was known, and not known, about the ground. That is the risk you carry every time you build on a shallow foundation. The broad facts below are well documented; consult the engineering literature for detail before you quote specifics.

Step 1: Timeline

The Transcona Grain Elevator was built near Winnipeg, Manitoba, by a railway company in the years before 1913, to store grain. It was a large block of reinforced concrete storage bins on a single thick foundation slab. In October 1913, as the bins were being filled with grain for the first time, the elevator began to settle and tilt. Within about a day it had leaned over at a dramatic angle, with one side sunk deep into the ground and soil heaved up beside it. Nobody died. Remarkably, the concrete structure stayed largely intact. It was later jacked back toward vertical and underpinned on new foundations carried down to firmer ground, and it went back into service for many years.

Step 2: Key decisions

The decisive choices were the foundation type and the bearing pressure. The designers placed a large, heavily loaded structure on a shallow foundation over clay, at a pressure that, when the bins were full, exceeded the clay's ultimate bearing capacity. The second decision was how much to investigate. The ground beneath was not explored to the depth the load would stress, so the weaker clay at depth was not properly characterised before design.

Step 3: Assumptions

The designers assumed that the ground could carry the load, based on information about the soil near the surface. A wide foundation, though, stresses soil far deeper than a narrow one, and the clay at depth was weaker than the assumption allowed. Later researchers studied the case and found that standard bearing capacity theory, applied with the clay's true strength, predicted the failure well. In other words, the tools to predict it existed; the data fed into them did not.

Say that out loud now.

Step 4: Incentives

A railway building grain storage wanted capacity in service before the harvest. Deeper investigation and deeper foundations cost money and time. A shallow slab on apparently firm ground was the cheapest, fastest answer. Nothing in the incentives rewarded looking deeper, and the cost of not looking was invisible until the bins were full.

Step 5: Warning signs ignored

Transcona failed fast, so the warning signs were mostly in the design stage rather than on site: a very wide, very heavily loaded foundation on clay, with limited knowledge of the clay below. On site, settlement began as the bins were filled, and the failure developed quickly once the load approached the soil's capacity. The lesson for warning signs is that a bearing failure often gives little time; the warning has to be heard on paper.

Step 6: Point of no return

The point of no return was the moment the full load of grain went into a foundation whose capacity had never been verified at depth. Filling in stages while monitoring settlement, and stopping at the first sign of accelerating movement, might have revealed the problem in time. Once the soil beneath one side began to fail in shear, it rotated and pushed the soil out sideways, and the structure followed.

Step 7: Root cause

The root cause was a foundation sized from a bearing value that had not been derived from the clay the load actually reached. The investigation did not match the building. The structure was right for the bearing value it was given; the bearing value was wrong for the ground.

What it means at small scale

Translate it to a hypothetical project. A developer builds a warehouse with a heavy racking load on a mat foundation, using a bearing value taken from a report prepared years earlier for a smaller building next door. The old borings went 6 metres deep; the new mat is 30 metres wide and stresses soil far deeper. The loads, the width and the depth all changed. The number was reused. That is Transcona with a different roof.

The cost comparison is stark. A second phase of deeper borings and a revised analysis might cost a hypothetical 30,000 dollars. Underpinning a tilted building, if it can be done at all, costs more than the original foundation many times over, plus the loss of use.

The prevention rule

Rule 110: Never size a foundation from a bearing value the geotechnical engineer did not derive for this site, these loads, this footing width and this depth, and never apply the full load to new or uncertain ground without monitoring its settlement first.

Professional sign-off required: licensed geotechnical engineer, for the investigation scope, the bearing pressure and the settlement prediction; structural engineer of record, for the foundation design.

Three questions to ask before the first footing

You do not need to repeat a bearing capacity calculation to apply Transcona. Ask three questions. First: was this bearing value derived for this building, or carried over from somewhere else? Second: how deep did the borings go, and how does that compare with the width of the widest foundation? Third: if the load goes on in stages, such as storage, water tanks or heavy equipment, is there a plan to measure settlement as the load builds, with a level at which loading stops?

The third question is the one most often skipped, and it is the one that could have saved Transcona. A structure that will be loaded heavily after completion, such as a warehouse, a water tank or a parking structure, can be monitored cheaply with survey points on the foundation, read as the load rises. Accelerating settlement under constant or slowly rising load is the classic sign that soil is approaching failure. Seen early, the load can be held while the engineer decides.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a reused or borrowed bearing value: from a neighbouring site, an older report, or a code table meant for small buildings. The control is a written confirmation from the geotechnical engineer that the recommended values were derived for the building as designed, with borings deep enough for its widest and most heavily loaded foundation.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner thinks a strong structure protects against a weak foundation. Transcona shows the opposite: the structure was strong enough to tip over in one piece.

Callback

In Week 2, Kema taught the outside view: judge a plan by how similar plans turned out. Foundations reward the habit. Ask the geotechnical engineer how buildings of this size and load on this soil have behaved nearby. A strong local reference class is often the best warning you will get.

Recap

In October 1913 the Transcona elevator tilted as it was first filled, because the clay beneath its wide foundation failed in bearing at a depth that had not been properly investigated. The structure survived and was righted on deeper foundations. Rule 110: size foundations only from values derived for this building, and monitor before full load.

Next: Sage on The Money: what foundation choices cost, and the value of knowing more about the ground.
checklist: I confirm that bearing values were derived for this building, not borrowed.
I check that borings reach the depth stressed by the widest, heaviest foundation.
I never reuse an old report for new loads without the geotechnical engineer's written review.
I consider staged loading and settlement monitoring for heavy loads on uncertain ground.
I ask for local reference cases of similar buildings on similar soil.
I treat accelerating settlement during loading as a stop signal.
head: Field checklist
speak: In October 1913 the newly built Transcona Grain Elevator near Winnipeg tilted dramatically as its bins were first filled with grain. Within about a day it leaned over with one side sunk deep into the clay. Nobody died, and the concrete structure stayed largely intact; it was later righted and underpinned on deeper foundations. The cause was a bearing failure: a very wide, heavily loaded foundation on clay that had not been investigated to the depth the load reached, at a pressure above the clay's capacity. Later study showed standard theory predicted the failure once the true clay strength was used. The tools existed; the data did not. So my rule is Rule 110: never size a foundation from a bearing value that was not derived for this site, these loads, this footing width and this depth, and never apply full load to uncertain ground without monitoring settlement first.
terms: Bearing capacity failure — the soil beneath a foundation failing in shear and pushing out sideways, so the foundation sinks and tilts.
Mat foundation — a single thick slab supporting a whole building, spreading its load over a wide area.
Underpinning — strengthening or deepening an existing foundation, usually by carrying its load down to firmer ground.

hostile.q: The neighbouring building's report gives a good bearing value, and that building is fine. Why are you paying for new borings?
hostile.a: Because that value was derived for that building's loads, footing widths and depth. Our foundation is wider and heavier, so it stresses soil much deeper than their borings reached. A bearing value only holds for the conditions it was calculated for. New borings to the right depth cost a small fraction of the foundation, and a fraction of a fraction of what underpinning would cost if the borrowed number were wrong.

rule: Rule 110: Never size a foundation from a bearing value the geotechnical engineer did not derive for this site, these loads, this footing width and this depth, and never apply the full load to new or uncertain ground without monitoring its settlement first.

title: What Foundations Cost, and What It Is Worth to Know More About the Ground
summary: Foundation choice moves cost, schedule and risk more than its share of the budget suggests. This lesson compares spread footings, ground improvement, a mat and piles with hypothetical numbers, prices the value of a second phase of investigation, and shows how settlement risk reaches value. Warrick's Wealth Ledger closes it.
body:
The cheapest foundation is the one that suits the ground you actually have. Money spent finding out what that ground is usually returns many times over, because it narrows the range of outcomes before the most expensive decisions are fixed.

Recall

Q. What does Rule 110 require of a bearing value?

A. That it was derived by the geotechnical engineer for this site, these loads, this footing width and this depth, with settlement monitored before full load on uncertain ground.

Q. What are the four channels from a design decision to value?

A. Capital cost, operating cost, revenue and risk.

Q. What is a standpipe system?

A. Fixed piping with hose connections on each floor, usually in the stairs, that gives firefighters a water supply inside the building without laying hose from the street.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, foundations are often under a tenth of hard cost, yet a wrong choice can add months, trigger redesign and, in the worst case, damage the building permanently. Investors and lenders know this. They will ask what you know about the ground, how confident you are, and what you have carried for the unknown.

Four options, priced

Take a hypothetical building with a footprint of 2,000 square metres and column loads suited to spread footings on good ground. The geotechnical report says the upper 2 metres is variable fill over stiff clay. Hypothetical, all-in costs:

OptionCostTimeSettlement risk
Spread footings on the fill300,000 dollars4 weeksHigh: the fill is variable
Remove fill, replace with engineered fill, then footings480,000 dollars7 weeksLow, if compaction is proven
Mat foundation650,000 dollars6 weeksLow differential, moderate total
Piles to the clay900,000 dollars8 weeksVery low

The cheapest option is not available, because the geotechnical engineer will not accept footings on variable fill. The real choice is between the second option at 480,000 dollars and the alternatives. That is why the investigation's description of the fill, how deep and how variable it is, is worth money: if the fill is 1 metre rather than 2, the replacement cost falls by about half.

Worked example: the value of a second investigation

Suppose the first-phase borings are widely spaced and the fill depth is uncertain: it could be 1 metre, with probability 50 percent, or 3 metres, with probability 50 percent. Replacement costs 360,000 dollars for 1 metre and 600,000 dollars for 3 metres; at 3 metres the engineer might instead prefer piles at 900,000 dollars.

Without more information, you must design for the worse case, because you cannot know which you have until you dig. Say you carry 900,000 dollars and design piles to be safe.

A second phase of closely spaced borings and test pits costs a hypothetical 25,000 dollars and two weeks. If it shows 1 metre of fill, you choose replacement at 360,000 dollars and save 540,000 dollars against the safe design. If it shows 3 metres, you choose replacement at 600,000 dollars, if the engineer accepts it, or piles. The expected saving is roughly half of 540,000, about 270,000 dollars, before counting the 3-metre case. Against a cost of 25,000 dollars, information that changes the decision is extraordinarily cheap.

Say that out loud now.

The general principle has a name: the value of information. Information is worth paying for when it could change a decision, and worth more the bigger the difference between the choices it decides between. Information that cannot change a decision is worth nothing, however interesting.

How settlement reaches value

Settlement problems rarely collapse a building. They show up as cracked finishes, sticking doors, sloping floors, leaking joints at the envelope and distorted lift shafts. Each becomes a repair cost, a tenant complaint and, at sale, a line in the buyer's survey. A buyer who sees ongoing settlement will either discount the price or demand a monitoring programme and an escrow. On a hypothetical building worth 30,000,000 dollars, a buyer's discount of 2 percent for foundation uncertainty is 600,000 dollars, more than the difference between the cheapest and safest foundation in the table.

Wealth Ledger

Warrick's note for your personal balance sheet: foundation problems are slow and long-lived, so they hurt the owner who holds. If you plan to keep a building for income and pass it on, the foundation is the last place to accept residual risk, because the cost appears in year five or year fifteen, after the construction lender is gone and the warranty has expired. Treat foundation quality as protection of the long-term asset in your estate, not as a construction line item.

Schedule as well as cost

Foundation choice also moves time, and time has a price. In the table, piles take eight weeks against seven for fill replacement, but piles need a specialist rig, mobilisation and often load testing before production, while fill replacement depends on dry weather and testing each lift. On a project carrying a hypothetical 150,000 dollars a week in interest, overheads and lost rent at the far end, a two-week difference in the foundation stage is worth 300,000 dollars if it lies on the critical path. That can reverse a ranking based on capital cost alone, in either direction.

Ask your scheduler to show the foundation options on the critical path, with their weather and testing risk, before the foundation type is fixed.

How the best price ground risk

Experienced owners and contractors price foundations as a range, not a number. A common practice is to carry the expected cost plus a contingency sized from the gap between the base case and a defined downside, and to state the assumptions that bound it: the depth of fill, the founding level, the groundwater level. When the investigation narrows the range, the contingency is released or reallocated. A small developer can copy this simply: for each foundation option, write the base and downside cost and the assumption that separates them, and show the lender the table.

That table also disciplines the design team. If the downside case is driven by one uncertain number, such as the fill depth, everyone can see that the cheapest way to reduce the contingency is to measure that number, not to argue about it.

Saying it to an investor

Put the money case in three sentences. "The fill depth was the swing factor between a 360,000-dollar replacement and a 900,000-dollar piled foundation. We spent 25,000 dollars to measure it before deciding. The result let us choose the cheaper foundation with a settlement prediction the engineers accept." An investor hears that you bought certainty at the right moment, which is the skill they are paying a developer for.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is choosing a foundation on capital cost alone after a thin investigation, and carrying no allowance for the case where the ground is worse than the borings suggest. The control is to buy the information that could change the foundation decision before it is fixed, and to price the residual uncertainty as a named contingency.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner treats the site investigation as a fixed fee to minimise. It is the one consultant spend that most often pays back many times over, because it narrows the range of the most expensive irreversible decision on the job.

Callback

In Week 44, Roman taught base, downside and severe cases. Foundations are a natural place to run them: the base case is the ground the report describes, the downside is fill twice as deep, and the severe case is a soft layer nobody found. Put the cost of each in the stress test before you commit.

Recap

Foundation choice should follow the ground: footings, replacement fill, a mat or piles. Pay for information that could change the decision; its value is the difference it makes times its probability. Settlement reaches value through repairs, complaints and the buyer's discount, and it hurts the long-term holder most.

Next: Ivo on The Rules: the code's foundation chapter, what the geotechnical report must contain, special inspections and who carries ground risk in the contract.
checklist: I compare foundation options by cost, time and settlement risk, not cost alone.
I ask what further investigation would change the foundation decision.
I pay for information when its expected saving exceeds its cost.
I carry a named contingency for ground worse than the borings suggest.
I consider how a buyer would price foundation uncertainty at sale.
I treat foundation quality as protection of the long-term asset.
head: Field checklist
speak: Foundations are a small share of cost but a large share of risk, and the right choice follows the ground. In my example, footings on variable fill are not acceptable, so the choice is between replacing the fill, a mat or piles, at 480,000, 650,000 and 900,000 dollars. The depth of the fill decides it, which is why more information is so valuable. If the fill could be 1 metre or 3, I would otherwise design for the worst case. A second investigation at 25,000 dollars that could save 540,000 is extraordinarily cheap. That is the value of information: it is worth paying for only when it can change a decision. Settlement rarely collapses buildings, but it shows up as cracks, complaints and a buyer's discount, and a 2 percent discount on a 30,000,000-dollar building is 600,000 dollars. Foundation risk lands on the long-term holder, so I buy information before I fix the foundation.
terms: Value of information — the expected improvement in a decision from gaining information, worth paying for only when it could change the choice.
Engineered fill — soil placed and compacted to a specification and tested, so it can support foundations.
Test pit — a shallow excavation dug to see and sample the soil directly, often used to map fill depth.

hostile.q: You want another 25,000 dollars for more borings when you already have a geotechnical report. Why should the equity pay for that?
hostile.a: Because the existing borings leave the fill depth uncertain between about 1 and 3 metres, and that difference decides between a 360,000-dollar replacement and a 900,000-dollar piled foundation. Without the information, prudence forces the expensive design. With it, there is roughly a one-in-two chance of saving about 540,000 dollars. The 25,000 dollars is the highest-return spend in the budget.

title: The Rules Beneath the Footing: Foundation Code, Special Inspections and Ground Risk
summary: The building code's chapter on soils and foundations sets when a geotechnical investigation is required, what it must cover, and when presumptive values may be used. Special inspections verify soils and fill. The contract decides who pays when the ground differs. This lesson walks through all three, with flags on what to verify.
body:
The code tells you the minimum the ground must be shown to do, the special inspector proves it was done, and the contract decides who pays when the ground turns out to be different. An owner needs all three in place before the first footing is dug.

Recall

Q. What is the value of information?

A. The expected improvement in a decision from gaining information; it is worth paying for only when it could change the choice.

Q. What does the building permit approve?

A. The construction documents as submitted and reviewed for code compliance; it does not certify the design is error-free.

Q. What is a performance-based fire design?

A. A design that meets the code's fire safety intent by engineering analysis rather than prescriptive rules, approved as an alternative method and often carrying permanent conditions.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, the rules around foundations are not mainly about the footing's shape. They are about evidence: what investigation the code requires, what the report must state, who inspects the soil and the fill, and how the contract treats ground that differs from the report. Each is a place where a missing document becomes a stopped job or a disputed claim.

The code's foundation chapter

In the International Building Code (IBC), soils and foundations are covered in their own chapter, Chapter 18 in recent editions. In broad terms it addresses when a geotechnical investigation is required, what the investigation and report should cover, excavation, grading and fill, load-bearing values of soils, and the design of shallow and deep foundations, with loads from ASCE 7 and concrete design to ACI 318 [unverified — confirm independently the exact scope and section structure in your adopted edition].

The building official may require a geotechnical investigation, and commonly does for anything beyond small buildings or where questionable soils, expansive soils, high groundwater or seismic concerns exist. The report is typically expected to describe the soils, groundwater, the bearing pressure and settlement recommendations, compaction requirements for fill, and any special conditions. Verify against the current adopted edition before relying on any provision.

The code also carries a table of presumptive load-bearing values for broad soil classes, usable in limited circumstances without a full investigation [unverified — confirm independently when your jurisdiction permits it]. These values are conservative defaults for simple cases. They are not a substitute for a site-specific report on a building of any size, and Rule 110 forbids treating them as one.

Say that out loud now.

Special inspections for soils

The code's special inspection requirements typically include soils work: verifying that the excavation for footings reaches the right depth and material, that the subgrade is as the report expected, and that fill is placed and compacted as specified, with testing [unverified — confirm independently the items your adopted edition lists]. The geotechnical engineer's representative or a qualified testing agency usually does this, engaged by the owner, and records each observation and test.

Worked example. A hypothetical project has 40 footings. The special inspector must observe each footing excavation before concrete. On day three, the crew digs footing 17 and finds soft, dark organic soil at the founding level, not the stiff clay in the report. The inspector records it and stops the pour at that footing. The geotechnical engineer instructs over-excavation to stiff clay, 1.2 metres deeper, and backfill with lean concrete. The cost is perhaps a hypothetical 6,000 dollars and a day. Without the inspection, the footing would have been poured on organic soil and settled for years.

Who pays when the ground differs

Ground risk is allocated by contract, and the allocation is commercial practice, not a code. The common tools are these.

A differing site conditions clause, found in many standard owner-contractor forms, compensates the contractor when conditions are materially different from those indicated in the contract documents, or from those ordinarily encountered for the kind of work. The wording varies by form and edition, so read yours. A geotechnical baseline report, or GBR, is a contractual statement of the ground conditions the parties agree to assume, for example "fill up to 2 metres deep" or "groundwater at 3 metres". Conditions worse than the baseline are the owner's; conditions within it are the contractor's. Baselines are common on tunnels and large earthworks and useful on any site with real ground risk.

Second worked example. A baseline says fill depth is up to 2 metres. On site the fill reaches 3 metres under one corner, adding 300 cubic metres of replacement at 60 dollars, 18,000 dollars. Under the baseline, the extra metre is the owner's cost, but the claim is clean: the baseline defines it, and there is no argument about what was foreseeable. Without a baseline, the same 18,000 dollars can become a dispute costing more than the work.

Reliance on the report

A geotechnical report is written for a client under an engagement with limits on who may rely on it. A lender, a contractor or a future buyer generally cannot rely on it unless the engineer grants reliance, usually by a reliance letter. Ask for reliance in your name, your entity's name and your lender's name at the start, and understand the engineer's limitation of liability.

Professional sign-off required: licensed geotechnical engineer, for the investigation, report and soils inspection; structural engineer of record, for the foundation design and the statement of special inspections; a construction lawyer, for the differing site conditions clause and any baseline.

Records that outlast the job

The foundation records are the ones you will be asked for longest: the geotechnical report and its addenda, the special inspector's footing observations, every compaction test with its location and lift, the geotechnical engineer's site instructions, and any settlement monitoring. Keep them in the owner's permanent file, indexed by footing and by grid line. When a crack appears in year eight, the first question an engineer asks is what the ground was and what was proved under that column, and the only good answer is a record made at the time.

Insist that the testing agency's reports state the test method, the specified target, the result as relative compaction and the location in plan and depth. A test report without a location is a number about nowhere.

Finally, put the code basis for the foundation in the architect's code analysis: the adopted edition, whether a geotechnical investigation was required, and the special inspection items for soils. When the building official or a buyer's engineer asks, the answer is in one place, dated and signed.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a foundation poured on ground nobody looked at, because special inspection of footing excavations was skipped to keep the pour sequence moving. The control is a hold point: no concrete in any footing until the special inspector has observed and recorded the founding level, and the record is in the project file that day.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner gives the contractor the geotechnical report "for information only" and assumes that shifts the ground risk. It may not, depending on the contract, and it can invite argument about what the contractor was entitled to rely on. Decide deliberately whether to use a baseline, and say so in the contract.

Callback

In Week 78, LEX taught risk allocation, including unforeseen ground. This lesson makes it concrete: the baseline report turns "unforeseen" from an argument into a measurement. The fill was either deeper than 2 metres or it was not.

Recap

The code's foundation chapter sets when an investigation is required, what it covers and when presumptive values may be used, which is rarely on a real building. Special inspections prove the founding soil and fill. The contract allocates ground risk; a differing site conditions clause and a baseline make it clean. Get reliance on the report for yourself and your lender.

Next: Bram on The Numbers: reverse engineering a footing and a compaction test from the finished result.
checklist: I know whether my jurisdiction requires a geotechnical investigation for this building.
I never use presumptive bearing values in place of a site-specific report.
My statement of special inspections covers footing excavations and fill.
No footing is poured until the special inspector records the founding level.
I have decided deliberately whether to use a differing site conditions clause and a baseline.
I have reliance on the geotechnical report for my entity and my lender.
head: Field checklist
speak: The code's foundation chapter, Chapter 18 of the IBC in recent editions, sets when a geotechnical investigation is required, what the report covers and when presumptive load-bearing values may be used, which on a real building is rarely, and I confirm the details in my adopted edition. Special inspections cover soils: the inspector observes each footing excavation and the placement and testing of fill, engaged by me and independent of the contractor. No footing is poured until the founding level is recorded. Ground risk is allocated by contract. A differing site conditions clause pays the contractor when the ground is materially different, and a geotechnical baseline report states the conditions the parties assume, so a claim becomes a measurement instead of an argument. And because a report is written for one client, I get a reliance letter for my entity and my lender at the start.
terms: Presumptive load-bearing values — conservative default soil pressures in the code, usable only in limited cases without a site-specific investigation.
Geotechnical baseline report (GBR) — a contractual statement of the ground conditions the parties agree to assume for allocating risk.
Reliance letter — a letter from a consultant allowing a named party, such as a lender, to rely on its report.

hostile.q: Your contractor found organic soil under one footing and wants 6,000 dollars and a day. Isn't that the contractor's risk?
hostile.a: It depends on the contract, and ours is clear. The baseline report describes stiff clay at founding level, and organic soil is materially different, so the extra excavation is our cost under the differing site conditions clause. I am glad to pay it: the special inspector found it before the pour, which is exactly what we pay inspection for. Six thousand dollars now is far cheaper than a footing that settles for years.

title: Reverse Engineering a Footing and a Compaction Test from the Finished Result
summary: An even-week reverse calculation. Start from a finished footing on the drawings and work back to the bearing pressure it implies, then check it against the report. Start from a field density result and work back to whether the fill passed. Hypothetical round numbers and units throughout.
body:
You do not need to design a footing to audit one. Work backward from what is drawn to the pressure it puts on the ground, and you can see in two lines whether it matches what the geotechnical engineer allowed.

Recall

Q. What is a geotechnical baseline report?

A. A contractual statement of the ground conditions the parties agree to assume, so that worse conditions are clearly the owner's risk and conditions within it are the contractor's.

Q. In the reverse-engineered design budget, how was hard cost found?

A. By taking maximum total cost from NOI over required yield on cost, subtracting land and finance, and solving for hard cost with percentage-based soft costs and contingency inside the equation.

Q. What does a fire alarm's notification system do?

A. It warns occupants through audible and visible signals, and in some buildings voice messages, so they know to leave or take protective action.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, drawings and reports are produced by different people, and the place they most often disagree is the footing schedule. A quick backward check lets you ask a sharp question before concrete goes in, without pretending to be the engineer. The answer always belongs to the structural engineer of record, but the question can come from you.

Units first

Force is measured in kilonewtons (kN). Pressure is force per area, in kilopascals (kPa), where 1 kPa is 1 kN per square metre. A column load on a drawing is usually given as a service load, the expected load in use, and the report's allowable bearing pressure is usually compared with service loads. Confirm which basis your engineer uses; mixing service and factored loads is a classic error.

Reverse calculation 1: from footing to pressure

Start with the finished outcome. The footing schedule shows footing F3 under a column with a service load of 1,800 kN. F3 is 3.0 metres by 3.0 metres, 0.8 metres thick, with its base 1.5 metres below finished ground.

Step 1. Footing area: 3.0 times 3.0 equals 9.0 square metres.

Step 2. Add the footing's own weight. Concrete weighs about 24 kN per cubic metre. Volume: 9.0 times 0.8 equals 7.2 cubic metres. Weight: 7.2 times 24, about 173 kN.

Step 3. Add the soil above the footing, between the top of the footing and the ground: 0.7 metres deep over the footing area, less the column, call it 9.0 times 0.7, which is 6.3 cubic metres, at about 18 kN per cubic metre, about 113 kN.

Step 4. Total load on the ground: 1,800 plus 173 plus 113 equals 2,086 kN.

Step 5. Gross bearing pressure: 2,086 divided by 9.0, about 232 kPa.

Now compare. Many reports state the allowable value as a net pressure, meaning the pressure above the weight of soil that was already there before excavation. The soil removed down to 1.5 metres weighed about 1.5 times 18, which is 27 kPa. Net pressure is about 232 minus 27, which is 205 kPa.

If the report's allowable net pressure is 150 kPa for settlement, F3 is about 37 percent over. That is a question for the structural engineer that afternoon: "F3 back-calculates to about 205 kPa net against a report allowable of 150. Am I reading the basis correctly?"

Say that out loud now.

Reverse calculation 2: what footing would have worked

Work it the other way. To keep net pressure at 150 kPa, roughly, the required area is the net load divided by 150. The net load is the total of 2,086 kN less the weight of soil removed over the footing area. Solving exactly needs iteration because the area changes the weights, but a first estimate is 1,800 kN plus a small allowance, say 1,880 kN, divided by 150, about 12.5 square metres, a footing about 3.55 metres square. A 3.6-metre square footing is about 44 percent more area and roughly 44 percent more concrete than F3. That is what the settlement limit costs, and it is far cheaper than the settlement.

Reverse calculation 3: from a test result to pass or fail

Now compaction. The specification requires structural fill compacted to at least 95 percent of the maximum dry density from the modified Proctor test, ASTM D1557. Verify against the current adopted edition and the project specification.

The laboratory reports a maximum dry density of 2.10 tonnes per cubic metre, at an optimum moisture content of 8 percent.

The field technician reports a wet density of 2.14 tonnes per cubic metre and a moisture content of 10 percent on lift 4.

Step 1. Convert wet density to dry density: dry density equals wet density divided by 1 plus the moisture content. 2.14 divided by 1.10 equals about 1.945 tonnes per cubic metre.

Step 2. Relative compaction equals dry density divided by maximum dry density. 1.945 divided by 2.10 equals about 0.926, or 92.6 percent.

Step 3. Compare: 92.6 is below 95. Lift 4 fails.

Step 4. Reverse engineer the cause. The moisture is 10 percent, 2 points wet of optimum. Wet fill is hard to compact, so the likely remedy is to scarify the lift, dry it toward optimum and recompact, then retest. To pass, dry density must reach 0.95 times 2.10, which is 1.995 tonnes per cubic metre.

The trap: a field report showing only the wet density of 2.14 looks higher than the laboratory maximum of 2.10 and seems to pass. Always compare dry with dry.

Reverse calculation 4: how many tests is enough

A last backward check, on frequency. Suppose the specification requires one compaction test for every 500 square metres of each 300-millimetre lift, with at least one test per lift per day, and the engineered fill area is 2,000 square metres, built in five lifts. Tests per lift: 2,000 divided by 500 equals 4. Total: 4 times 5 equals 20 tests, at a hypothetical 150 dollars each, 3,000 dollars. If the testing invoice shows 8 tests, you know before you pay it that the fill has not been proven to the specification. Ask which lifts were untested before anything else is built on them.

Frequencies like these are set by the project specification and the geotechnical engineer, often informed by agency or industry guidance; they are not universal numbers. The method of the check is universal: divide the area and the lifts by the frequency, and compare with the count of tests actually reported.

Taken together, the four reverse checks give you a short owner's audit of any foundation package: pressure against allowable, footing size against load, relative compaction against target, and test count against frequency. None replaces the engineers. All of them let you ask the right question on the right day.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a footing schedule and a geotechnical report that were never reconciled, especially on the basis of the pressure, gross or net, and the load, service or factored. The control is a one-page reconciliation by the structural engineer, listing each footing's back-calculated pressure against the report's allowable, issued before the foundation drawings are released.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner compares a wet field density with a dry laboratory maximum and passes a failed lift. Ask for relative compaction as a percentage, calculated on dry density, on every test report.

Callback

In Week 109, Quincy taught the three volumes of soil: bank, loose and compacted. Compaction testing is the last of the three made measurable. The compacted volume is only real when a test shows the density was reached.

Recap

Back-calculate a footing's pressure from the column load, the footing and soil weights and the area, then compare on the same basis, net or gross, service or factored, with the report. Size a footing by dividing the load by the allowable. Calculate relative compaction from dry density against the laboratory maximum, and diagnose a failure from the moisture.

Next: Greta on The Room: the morning the compaction tests fail under the footings and the concrete trucks are booked.
checklist: I know whether the report's allowable bearing pressure is net or gross.
I know whether column loads on the drawings are service or factored loads.
I can back-calculate a footing's bearing pressure from its load and size.
I ask the structural engineer for a footing-by-footing reconciliation with the report.
I check relative compaction is calculated on dry density.
I diagnose failed compaction from the moisture content before allowing rework.
head: Field checklist
speak: I can audit a footing by working backward. Footing F3 carries a service load of 1,800 kilonewtons on a 3 by 3 metre base, 9 square metres. Add the footing's own weight, about 173 kilonewtons, and the soil above it, about 113, for 2,086 in total. That is about 232 kilopascals gross. Take off the soil originally there, about 27, and it is about 205 net. If the report allows 150 net for settlement, F3 is about 37 percent over, and I ask the structural engineer whether I am reading the basis right. A footing at 150 needs about 12.5 square metres, roughly 3.6 metres square. For compaction, a wet density of 2.14 at 10 percent moisture is a dry density of about 1.945, which is 92.6 percent of a 2.10 maximum, so it fails 95. The moisture is 2 points wet of optimum, so the fix is to dry and recompact. Always compare dry with dry.
terms: Kilopascal (kPa) — a unit of pressure equal to one kilonewton per square metre.
Net bearing pressure — the pressure under a footing above the weight of soil that was there before excavation.
Relative compaction — field dry density divided by the laboratory maximum dry density, expressed as a percentage.

hostile.q: Your field report shows 2.14 tonnes per cubic metre against a laboratory maximum of 2.10. That is over 100 percent. Why are you rejecting the lift?
hostile.a: Because 2.14 is a wet density and the laboratory maximum is a dry density. At 10 percent moisture, the dry density is about 1.945, which is 92.6 percent of maximum, below the 95 percent specified. The fill is also 2 points wet of optimum, which explains it. The lift gets dried, recompacted and retested before anything goes on top of it.

title: The Morning the Tests Fail and the Trucks Are Booked
summary: A realistic scene on site at 6:30 in the morning: compaction tests under three footings have failed, concrete trucks are booked for 8:00, and the contractor wants to pour and test later. Learn the lines to say, the lines never to say, the question behind the question, and how to hold your state. A short thread on founder health closes it.
body:
When a test fails on the morning of a pour, the decision is not whether the test was annoying. It is whether you are willing to bury a known defect under concrete. You are not, and you can say so calmly and quickly.

Recall

Q. How do you calculate relative compaction from a field test?

A. Convert the field wet density to dry density by dividing by 1 plus the moisture content, then divide by the laboratory maximum dry density.

Q. In the design stage gate mock meeting, what did you do when the fire engineer quietly raised a coordination problem?

A. Thanked them in front of the room, gave the interface one owner, and required it resolved before permit.

Q. What is a fire pump's churn condition?

A. The pump running with no flow, at its maximum pressure, which the fire protection design must account for so the system is not over-pressured.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, here is the scene. It is 6:30 in the morning. Six footings were excavated yesterday on engineered fill. The special inspector's technician tested the fill under all six last evening; three failed, at 92 to 93 percent against 95. The concrete supplier has 12 trucks booked for 8:00. The pump is already on site. The contractor's superintendent, the technician, your project manager and you are standing at the site office. The geotechnical engineer is on the phone.

Scene one: "Pour now, test later"

The superintendent says: "Those tests are marginal. The fill's been rolled to death. Let's pour all six, and if anything shows up we'll deal with it."

The question behind the question: is the owner going to let schedule pressure override a hold point?

Say: "I hear you, and I know what a lost pour costs. But those three footings are on fill that has not met the specification, and once the concrete is in, we cannot test or fix what is under it. Let us pour the three that passed this morning, and fix the other three today."

Never say: "Ninety-three is close enough." It may be, but that is the geotechnical engineer's call, and once you say it, you have made yourself the engineer of record for the fill.

Then turn to the phone: "Greta, can you tell us what you want done on the three failed footings, and whether pouring the three passed ones this morning affects anything?"

And then stay silent while she answers. The engineer's instruction is what the record needs.

Say that out loud now.

Scene two: the cause

The technician says the failed lifts were wet, 2 to 3 points over optimum, after rain two nights ago.

Say: "Thank you, that is useful. Greta, is drying and recompacting the top lift the fix, or do you want those lifts removed?" She says to scarify, dry and recompact the top 300 millimetres and retest, and if the moisture cannot be brought down today, to replace the top lift with drier imported material.

Turn to the superintendent: "Can your crew do that this morning, and can we retest by early afternoon? If they pass, we pour the three tomorrow."

The question behind this is the superintendent's: who pays? Have the answer ready. "Under the specification, the contractor places and compacts fill to 95 percent, so rework of failed lifts is in your scope. If you believe the rain was a delay event, put it in a notice and we will deal with it under the contract."

Never say: "We'll cover it, just get it done." That pays for rework the contract already allocates and sets a precedent for every failed test after this one.

Scene three: the trucks

The superintendent: "If we only pour three, we pay for nine trucks we don't use."

Have the number. Twelve trucks at 8 cubic metres is 96 cubic metres; six footings of about 7 cubic metres each need about 42. Twelve trucks were booked because the contractor planned a slab section too. Say: "Let us recount. Three footings is about 21 cubic metres, three trucks. Can the supplier release the rest at short notice? If there is a cancellation charge, it goes in the daily record, and we will see under the contract whose it is."

A worked comparison worth saying: a cancellation charge for nine trucks might be a few thousand dollars. A footing that settles 30 millimetres more than its neighbour can cost a hypothetical 80,000 dollars or more to underpin later, if it can be reached at all. Say it plainly and without drama.

Closing the morning

Read back, and write it in the daily record: "F1, F2 and F5 passed and pour this morning, with inspector release. F3, F4 and F6 failed at 92 to 93 percent, wet of optimum. Geotechnical engineer instructs scarify, dry and recompact the top 300 millimetres, retest this afternoon; replace with imported material if moisture cannot be reduced. No concrete on F3, F4, F6 until passed and released."

Holding your state

This conversation happens early, often after little sleep, with engines running and people impatient. Slow your speech. Breathe out longer than you breathe in once before you answer the first push, standing still and parked, not walking across the site. Keep your sentences short. The superintendent is not your opponent; the clock is. Treat the superintendent as an ally against the clock, and they usually become one.

Founder health, a monthly thread

Early pours, night shifts and long site days can stack up. Plan your sleep around the critical site mornings as you would plan the pour itself, and keep the caffeine for the first half of the day. These are general habits, not medical advice; check with your doctor about sleep, caffeine and shift work for your own health.

A clear head at 6:30 is a control on the project. The decision you make on a failed test is permanent, and you want to make it rested.

What to do the next morning

The decision is only half the work. The next morning, check three things before the second pour. The retest results for F3, F4 and F6, calculated as relative compaction on dry density. The special inspector's written release for each footing. And the weather forecast: if rain is due before the concrete can go in, the subgrade may need protecting with a blinding layer of lean concrete or a cover, or it will need testing again. Ask the superintendent what the plan is if it rains, and listen to the answer.

Then look at the pattern. Three failures in six on wet fill after rain says the earthworks sequence is exposed to weather. A sentence in the next site meeting about protecting completed lifts may save the next failed morning.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is pouring over a failed or untested subgrade because the trucks are already on the road. The control is a written hold point, released only by the special inspector, and a standing rule that a booked truck is never a reason to pour.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner tries to negotiate a compromise on site, such as pouring all six and adding a monitoring point. Compromises on buried work are rarely compromises; they are deferrals of a cost you can no longer see.

Callback

In Week 109's pre-excavation meeting, Duke taught that the stop decision should sit with someone independent of the schedule. A hold point on footing subgrade is the same control at a smaller scale: the special inspector's release, not the superintendent's confidence, opens the pour.

Recap

Pour what passed, fix what failed, and never bury a known defect. Get the geotechnical engineer's instruction on the record, know the cause, know who pays under the contract, and have the cost comparison ready. Close by writing the decisions in the daily record, and make the call rested.

Next: Kema on Quiz and Recap: the week on shallow foundations, with a Red Pen drill on a geotechnical report excerpt.
checklist: I never let a booked truck be the reason to pour.
I pour only footings released by the special inspector.
I get the geotechnical engineer's instruction on the record for every failed test.
I know the cause of the failure before agreeing the fix.
I know who pays for rework under the specification and the contract.
I have the cost comparison between a lost pour and later underpinning ready.
I write the morning's decisions in the daily record.
head: Field checklist
speak: When compaction tests fail on the morning of a pour, I will not bury a known defect. Three footings passed, so they pour once the inspector releases them. Three failed at 92 to 93 percent against 95, so they wait. I never say close enough, because that makes me the engineer. I put the geotechnical engineer on the record: scarify, dry and recompact the top 300 millimetres, and retest, or replace it with drier material. The cause is moisture after rain, and under the specification rework of failed fill is the contractor's scope; if they see a delay event, they give notice under the contract. I recount the trucks and cut the order to what we can pour, and I can say the comparison: a few thousand dollars of cancellation against the cost of underpinning a settled footing. Then I write it all in the daily record, and I make the call rested.
terms: Hold point — a stage in the work beyond which it may not proceed until a named person has inspected and released it.
Optimum moisture content — the moisture at which a soil reaches its maximum dry density under a given compaction effort.
Daily record — the site diary that records work, tests, instructions and decisions each day.

hostile.q: You've cost us a morning and nine trucks over a percent or two of compaction. Is that really worth it?
hostile.a: Yes, because the footings carry columns for the life of the building, and once the concrete is in we can neither test nor fix the fill under it. The geotechnical engineer specified 95 percent for a reason, and the cause is clear: the fill is wet. We poured what passed, the rest will pass this afternoon or tomorrow, and the truck charges are recorded for the contract to decide.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 110 Review: Bearing, Settlement, Investigation and Compaction
summary: Six questions test the week on shallow foundations: bearing versus settlement, reading a geotechnical report, the value of information, the foundation rules, the reverse footing check and the failed-test morning. A Red Pen drill on a hypothetical geotechnical report excerpt with planted defects follows, and a two-minute boardroom drill closes the week.
body:
This week came down to one sentence: a shallow foundation is only as good as what is known about the ground beneath it at the depth its load reaches, and what is proven about the fill it stands on.

Recall

Q. On the morning of a pour with failed compaction tests, what is never a reason to pour?

A. That the concrete trucks are already booked.

Q. What does Rule 109 require of temporary works that hold back ground or water?

A. A named designer, an independent design check and a monitoring plan whose trigger levels stop the work, held by someone who does not own the schedule.

Q. In the design checkpoint, what order did the big design decisions lock in?

A. Use and occupancy, then construction type and height, then the flood and wind basis, then the structural grid and floor height, then stairs and shafts.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, foundations are where the cheapest mistakes on paper become the most expensive in the ground. If you can answer these six questions aloud without notes, you can read a geotechnical report, question a footing schedule and stand firm on a failed test. Answer each aloud before reading the answer.

The six questions

Question 1. What two limits govern a shallow foundation, and which usually decides?

Answer: Bearing capacity, the pressure at which the soil fails in shear, reduced by a factor of safety; and settlement, especially differential settlement between footings. On soft or variable ground, settlement usually governs.

Question 2. What do you check first in a geotechnical report?

Answer: The findings before the recommendations: how many borings, how deep, and whether they agree. Borings must reach the depth the foundation stresses, roughly one and a half to two footing widths, and deeper under a mat.

Question 3. What happened at Transcona, and what is Rule 110?

Answer: In October 1913 the elevator tilted as it was first filled, because the clay beneath its wide foundation failed in bearing at a depth not properly investigated. Rule 110: size foundations only from values derived for this site, these loads, this width and this depth, and monitor settlement before full load on uncertain ground.

Question 4. When is a further investigation worth paying for?

Answer: When it could change the foundation decision. Its value is the difference between the choices it decides, weighted by probability. In the example, 25,000 dollars of borings could save about 540,000.

Question 5. A field test shows a wet density of 2.14 against a laboratory maximum of 2.10. Pass?

Answer: Not necessarily. Convert to dry: at 10 percent moisture, 2.14 over 1.10 is about 1.945, which is 92.6 percent of 2.10. Against a 95 percent specification, it fails.

Question 6. Who pays when the ground differs from the report?

Answer: The contract decides. A differing site conditions clause compensates materially different conditions; a geotechnical baseline report defines the assumed conditions, so the claim becomes a measurement. These are commercial practice, not code.

Say that out loud now.

Red Pen drill

Read this hypothetical excerpt from a geotechnical report's recommendations. Find the defects before reading the answers.

Recommendations. Three borings were advanced to 5 metres. The site is suitable for spread footings or a mat foundation at an allowable bearing pressure of 250 kPa, based on the presumptive values in the building code. Settlement is not expected to be significant. Existing fill may be left in place below slabs. Groundwater was not encountered. Fill shall be compacted to a high standard. This report is for the exclusive use of the client and may be relied on by lenders and contractors.

The defects:

  1. Borings to 5 metres may not reach the depth stressed by a mat foundation, which loads soil much deeper than a footing.
  2. A bearing value based on code presumptive values, not site testing, contrary to Rule 110.
  3. No distinction between footings and a mat, which stress the ground very differently.
  4. "Settlement is not expected to be significant" gives no number for total or differential settlement.
  5. Leaving existing fill below slabs with no description of its depth or variability, and no testing.
  6. "Groundwater was not encountered" with no statement of when the borings were drilled or whether levels vary by season.
  7. "Compacted to a high standard" names no percentage, no laboratory test and no testing frequency.
  8. The reliance sentence contradicts itself: exclusive to the client, yet relied on by lenders and contractors, with no reliance letter.

Recap

A shallow foundation must not fail the ground and must not settle too much or unevenly; settlement usually governs. Read the logs, check the depth, and demand a settlement number. Buy information that could change the decision. The code requires an investigation and special inspections; the contract allocates ground risk. Back-calculate footings on the same basis as the report, compare dry density with dry, and never pour over a failed test.

Boardroom drill

Explain the week in two minutes to a lender's credit officer who asks, "How do you know the foundations are right, and what is your exposure if the ground is worse?" Set a timer and speak before reading the model answer.

Model answer: "Our foundations are sized from a geotechnical report derived for this building, with borings deep enough for our widest foundation, and the engineer has confirmed that in writing. The allowable pressure is governed by settlement, and the report gives total and differential settlement figures the structural engineer has accepted. We paid for a second phase of borings because the fill depth was the swing factor between replacing it and piling, and the result let us replace it. Every footing excavation and every fill lift is inspected and tested by an inspector we hired, and no concrete goes in until the inspector releases it. If the ground is worse than the baseline report, the contract makes that our cost, and we carry a named ground contingency for it. You have reliance on the report in your name."

Linking the week to the next

Next week moves to deep foundations, where the same questions return in a new form. A pile is still sized from a capacity derived for this site, this load and this depth; it is still proven by testing rather than assumed; and it still raises the question of who pays when it must be driven longer than planned. Keep Rule 110 in mind as you read: a pile capacity borrowed from another site is the same error as a borrowed bearing value.

Before you close the week, say Rules 108, 109 and 110 aloud in order, one breath each. If any of the three does not come out cleanly, reread its Day 2 lesson tonight.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk in reviewing this week is remembering the numbers and forgetting the depth. Every bearing value is only true for the soil it describes, to the depth it was measured. Ask about depth first, every time.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner reads the Red Pen answers before marking the excerpt. Mark it first, count what you found, and write that number in your decision journal beside last week's.

Scoring yourself

Six clear answers means you are ready for deep foundations next week. Four or five means reread the lesson behind each miss today. Fewer than four means rehearse the two limits, Rule 110 and the dry-density calculation aloud tomorrow and take the questions again. Most people miss the reliance contradiction and the missing groundwater timing in the Red Pen, because they read for engineering and skip the paperwork. Both decide money later.

Callback

In Week 108, the design checkpoint taught that design decisions lock in order and that changes must be re-checked as a whole. The foundation is the first locked decision that cannot be unlocked at all. Rule 108, Rule 109 and Rule 110 together guard the moment the drawings meet the ground.

checklist: Can I name the two limits on a shallow foundation and which usually governs?
Can I say what to check first in a geotechnical report?
Can I state Rule 110 and the Transcona facts?
Can I explain when further investigation is worth paying for?
Can I calculate relative compaction from a wet density and moisture content?
Can I explain how the contract allocates ground risk?
head: The six questions
speak: A shallow foundation is only as good as what is known about the ground at the depth its load reaches. Two limits govern it: bearing capacity, divided by a factor of safety, and settlement, especially differential settlement, which usually decides on soft or variable ground. I read the boring logs before the recommendations and check the borings reach the stressed depth, deeper under a mat. From Transcona in 1913, Rule 110: size foundations only from values derived for this site, these loads, this width and this depth, and monitor before full load. I pay for more investigation when it could change the decision. The code requires an investigation and special inspections of footings and fill; the contract allocates ground risk through a differing site conditions clause and a baseline. I back-calculate footings on the same basis as the report, compare dry density with dry, and never pour over a failed test.
terms: Allowable bearing pressure — the soil pressure a foundation may apply, limited by strength and by settlement.
Relative compaction — field dry density divided by laboratory maximum dry density, as a percentage.
Differing site conditions clause — a contract term compensating the contractor for ground materially different from what the documents indicated.

hostile.q: Your geotechnical engineer is reputable. Why do you need special inspections and your own checks on top of the report?
hostile.a: Because the report describes the ground at a few borings, and the special inspections confirm the ground at every footing and every fill lift. The report is a prediction; the inspection is the evidence. The code requires special inspection of soils work, I pay for it so it stays independent of the contractor, and no concrete goes in until it is released. That record is what lets you, and a future buyer, rely on the foundation.
